cur:manuscripts-drogo-ascension.summary: Inside the gold-and-vine initial C of the Ascension Day prayer, Christ strides up a hillside toward the sky, holding a staff, and grasps the hand of God reaching down from the clouds, while angels fly beside him. Below, the Virgin and the apostles look up in wonder. The lively, sketchy figures are typical of the Metz painters.
facts: Wikipedia describes this initial: Christ, holding a staff, accepts God's hand and begins his ascension into the clouds.
The Drogo Sacramentary was written and painted for the personal use of Drogo, Bishop of Metz and a son of Charlemagne; it contains only the prayers spoken by the bishop at Mass through the year.
cur:manuscripts-drogo-ascension.notes: The folio (71v) is given on other Commons files of this page.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: At the top of the miniature, the haloed Christ sits in a green medallion between two angels, while below him dragons, serpents, birds, beasts and cattle fill the earth and sea. The psalm calls every creature to praise: 'Praise the Lord from the earth, ye dragons, and all deeps … beasts, and all cattle; creeping things, and flying fowl'.
facts: Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

cur:monumental2-agacalti-flight-into-egy.summary: On a yellow ground framed by a white border, the Virgin sits on a pale donkey holding the Christ Child before her, while Joseph, leaning on a staff, walks at the left and a second haloed figure leads the animal at the right. Surrounded by losses in the plaster, this small panel near the dome preserves the simple, flat colours characteristic of the church.
facts: The paintings of Ağaçaltı combine figure scenes with dense geometric and textile-like ornament, one of the reasons scholars have found them difficult to date.
cur:monumental2-agacalti-flight-into-egy.notes: Date disputed: proposals range from the 7th century to the 10th–11th century. The faces are damaged and modern graffiti are scratched into the lower part.

cur:objects-coin-michael-iii-theodora-so.summary: The obverse shows the nimbate bust of Christ Pantokrator, raising his hand in blessing and holding the Gospels; the reverse shows the young emperor Michael III beside his mother, the regent Theodora, both crowned. Struck in the years after the end of Iconoclasm in 843, the coin announced across the empire that the image of Christ had been restored. The face of Christ returned to the coinage after an absence of nearly a century and a half.
facts: Wikipedia's article on Byzantine coinage notes that the type of Justinian II, with Christ on the obverse, was revived after the end of Iconoclasm and remained the norm until the end of the Empire.
Wikipedia notes that Theodora, as regent for Michael III, restored the veneration of icons in March 843, ending the second Byzantine Iconoclasm; she is venerated as a saint in the Orthodox Church.

Q116273260.summary: Carved around this small round ivory box, a youthful Christ sits enthroned at the centre, flanked by the bearded Saints Peter and Paul, while other disciples bring forward loaves of bread with baskets at their feet. The miracle of the loaves was understood by the early Church as a sign of the bread of the Eucharist, and such boxes may have served in the Divine Liturgy.
facts: According to the Met, the box was made in North Africa, while its lid was made in Spain.
Traces of polychromy survive, and coloured inlays decorate the lid.
It came to the Met in 1917 as a gift of J. Pierpont Morgan.
Q116273260.notes: The Met cites Mark 8:1–6 (feeding of the four thousand); the scene could equally evoke the feeding of the five thousand.
